title: Land Is Not a Commodity: Why a Land Value Tax Can Cure the Housing Crisis
dek: The housing shortage is only a symptom; the real disease is land monopoly. A land value tax shifts the burden off buildings and onto land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, and returning location value to society instead of fattening landlords.
why: The land value tax is an overlooked lever that economists on both left and right agree on. Lars Doucet turns an abstract tax regime into a power struggle, using Houston parking lots, South Korea's appraisal system, and Norway's resource dividend as cases.
who: Economists who care about housing policy, urban planners, real estate developers, and investors and policy researchers who want to know whether the land tax is worth betting on.

points.h: A land tax is not a property tax, it is a location tax
points.body: Lars builds his case on one analogy: the land value tax and the ordinary property tax share an origin, but the LVT splits ‘building value’ from ‘land value’. A building tax punishes you for constructing, maintaining, improving; a land tax only punishes you for occupying a good location and letting it sit fallow. Land value, he says, comes from the labor of the people around you — your ability to earn a living, go to school, make friends the moment you walk out the door depends on your neighbors and the whole city. The landlord lies back and sucks that collective value into his own pocket. That is the paradox of Progress and Poverty: the ballpoint pen fell from $270 to 11 cents, and land never does.

points.h: The YIMBYs are right, but not right enough
points.body: The host asks: Oakland upzoned and rents fell — do we still need a land tax? Lars concedes the ‘housing shortage’ is the main cause, but points out that YIMBYs never explain a counterexample: Houston has no zoning, yet its downtown still holds a giant surface parking lot worth $500 million. Why? Because the property tax bundles land and building together, so the more you build the more you owe, while sitting on it and waiting for appreciation is cheaper. So developers have no incentive to develop, only an incentive to lobby for rezoning and then keep hoarding. Without land tax reform, he says, you arrive at the stalemate of ‘you rezoned it, but I just won't sell’.

points.h: The objections are built on imagination
points.body: Lars sorts the opposition into three camps and dismantles each. How do you appraise land separately from buildings? He says 14,000 assessment jurisdictions worldwide already do something like it: South Korea manually reviews 500,000 sample parcels a year and produces nationwide land values in 5 months; Norway trained a national automated valuation model on the state property data platform Finn.no with a core team of just 3 people. Think there will be too many protests? He says the real source of protest is ‘the land looks the same as next door, why charge me more’ — under a land tax, you and your neighbor are assessed on the same location basis, which makes it easier, not harder. The excuse for not doing it is that nobody has measured it.

points.h: The little old lady is not an argument against it
points.body: The sharpest criticism is ‘the transition is unfair’ — on the day a land tax is announced, existing landowners instantly bear the capitalized burden of all future taxes, which amounts to expropriation in one stroke. Lars concedes this is a Gordon Tullock-style transition trap, then offers the guardrail: the move is never a one-step nationwide 100% land tax, but a gradual switchover by school district or county; run revenue-neutral simulations and most single-family homes see their tax bill fall. As for the elderly afraid of being driven out of the old family home, he says Texas has long had a tax deferral system: you owe it, and after death it is deducted with interest from the estate.

points.h: Britain's failure was a capacity problem
points.body: The most-cited counterexample online is Britain's 1910s ‘People's Budget’: the valuation took 6 years and was overturned by shopkeepers' protests and the courts. Lars's reply is blunt: the much-shared article is simply ‘deriving a universal law from one sample’, and it simultaneously claims that ‘a pure land tax has never succeeded’ and that ‘land cannot be valued’ — yet South Korea has been appraising nationwide land values parcel by parcel for decades. That proves only that the British state machine was weak, not that a land tax is theoretically unworkable. His tone hardens: if you want to be a serious critic, go find counterexamples, instead of passing off lazy ignorance as a settled verdict.

points.h: Norway achieved Georgism through a resource dividend
points.body: Lars points to a fact that makes Norway a ‘success story’ today: Norway's entire resource management regime is Georgist in structure — oil and other natural resources are deemed the property of all the people, and extractors pay extremely high resource taxes, while production and investment themselves are not punished, so entrepreneurship is encouraged and the natural bounty is captured for the treasury to fund universal welfare. Norway's Georgism is almost perfect, except that it is not on land value. This ‘Norwegian paradox’ leads him to assert: the land tax is not the enemy of the welfare state, it can be its foundation.

points.h: The automobile opened a second frontier
points.body: Lars explains why the land question that obsessed every city 100 years ago later vanished: the frontier is itself a mechanism of ‘free land’ — as long as you can still expand into the wilderness, the poor don't have to face the squeeze of ‘high wages plus high rent’. America's first frontier was westward expansion; when it closed, Henry George appeared. In the 20th century the automobile turned the suburbs into a ‘second frontier’ and extended the run another 80 years, until it closed again around 2006-2008. He says people now call this a ‘second Gilded Age’, but it is just the script from a hundred-odd years ago with a new cast, and post-pandemic remote work as a ‘third frontier’ held out for about 5 minutes before capital digested it.

points.h: Don't win online, do the politicians' homework
points.body: The closing answer is very practical: Lars says the most effective way to make change he has learned in the past 5 years is not arguing with keyboard warriors, but taking every objection a state senator or city council member might raise, running the data simulations and preparing the answers in advance, and putting them directly on their desks — ‘doing politicians' homework’, he says, is an absurd but extraordinarily effective strategy. A few states have already passed bills allowing land tax reform. His call to action: go measure, don't guess.

terms.def: An annual tax levied on the value of land rather than total property value, which does not punish building improvements.
The 19th-century movement launched by Henry George: land is common wealth, and land rent should be captured by society.
The movement that advocates loosening land-use zoning rules and allowing more housing to be built.
Using a unified model and sample parcels to value properties automatically across a whole jurisdiction, rather than assessing each one on site.
The Georgist ideal: tax only land value and abolish all other taxes on labor and capital.
The high rents extracted from natural resources (such as oil) and returned to all citizens.
